title: xtty — A terminal that makes everyday work easier
summary:
Spend your time on the work, not the terminal.

I'm the developer of xtty, a native macOS terminal for everyday shell, SSH and coding-agent work. The goal is to reduce repeated setup and switching between sessions, so you can stay focused on the work you opened the terminal to do.

Everyday workflows, in one terminal

  • Connect to servers: open several saved SSH hosts together, including configured jump-host routes.
  • Handle repeated password prompts: use configured matching rules and saved credentials for automatic filling.
  • Open another remote shell: Duplicate Tab starts a fresh, independent SSH connection to the same server and restores the remote working directory.
  • Move files: transfer files with sz/rz using native macOS file dialogs.
  • Work across sessions: arrange tabs and split panes, broadcast input to selected panes, and see coding-agent status indicators.

These features share one purpose: spend less time recreating the working environment and more time using it.

Watch the actual UI

A concrete example: opening a second SSH shell

Suppose a command is running on a server and you want a separate shell in the same project directory. Duplicate Tab opens another connection and restores that directory, while the original shell stays separate.

It does not clone running processes or preserve a session across disconnections. For persistent remote sessions, tools such as tmux address a different need. With broadcast input, check the selected destinations before entering commands.

Availability and tradeoffs

xtty is proprietary and macOS-only, with Apple Silicon and Intel downloads. There is a Free edition, a seven-day Pro trial, and an optional US$29.90 one-time Pro purchase. No subscription.

iTerm2 remains a mature, free, open-source choice. xtty focuses on making everyday connection, session and file-transfer workflows accessible directly in the UI.

title: Share a Kafka Topic Only When Order Matters
summary:
We merged Kafka topics because the same services consumed the messages together. It felt simpler. Two incidents showed what we had really done: one shared topic means one shared queue, one failure domain, and one on-call problem—not a tidy folder in a repo.

My default rule: share a topic only when order matters for a clear stream (same partition key, same lifecycle). If urgency, retries, batch vs live traffic, or ownership differ, split the topics. Below I explain why we merged, what broke in production, when one topic is still right, and defaults that help teams avoid the same mistakes.

Why we merged topics

We had several topics. The same services read the events. Dashboards grouped them. We used the same domain words (“orders,” “billing,” “notifications”). Merging felt reasonable:

  • Fewer topic names and fewer ACL/schema subjects to manage
  • One obvious place per business area
  • One mental pipeline for producers and consumers

We also followed a familiar rule of thumb: combine topics that are mostly consumed together. If the same consumers normally subscribe to all of them, one topic can be simpler. Consumers can skip message types they do not handle—that is acceptable. Fetching from Kafka is cheap; ignoring even a large share of messages on a topic is often not a big cost. You only need a separate topic when consumers would ignore the vast majority of messages.

We put message type in the header so each record could be parsed and routed to the right handler. That made “one topic, many processes” feel safe: separate code paths without separate topic names.

That made merging feel low-risk. The incidents below showed we had still missed something.

What that advice does not cover

Co-consumption answers who reads the stream. It does not spell out what guarantees the log must provide—ordering, retention, retries, and what happens when one message type misbehaves.

You can join streams in application code, materialized views, or analytics. A Kafka topic is not a join key. It is an append-only log with contracts for ordering and retention. Headers that distinguish message type help you dispatch inside the consumer; they do not give you separate partitions, consumer lag, or retry boundaries. When message types need different contracts, one topic still ties them together. You often only notice that under load or during failure—not when consumers happily skip or route messages in code.

Incident 1: Bulk traffic blocked important work

Setup. Topic billing.events, partition key accountId, already handled live payment-captured and invoice-issued. Later we added ledger-export-row to the same topic so the export job could reuse the same pipeline and accountId keying. One consumer group still processed every message type in partition order.

What happened. After ledger-export-row joined billing.events, a heavy export run—or backlog after an outage—filled partitions for busy accountId values. payment-captured and invoice-issued kept flowing as before, but new records queued behind export rows on the same partitions. The consumer could not prefer the live types that had been fine on their own; offset order now applied to ledger-export-row too. Lag on payment-captured and invoice-issued climbed while the group chewed through export rows at a fixed rate.

Symptoms.

  • End-to-end latency alerts on payment-captured / invoice-issued flows while ledger-export-row lag was high on billing.events
  • Support reports: payments or invoices “stuck for hours” with no export job visibly “broken”
  • Healthy brokers, growing consumer lag on the shared group consuming billing.events

Mitigation. We stopped the ledger-export-row producer, watched lag on billing.events, and waited until the consumer drained enough backlog that payment-captured and invoice-issued caught up. It worked, but only as a manual lever—identify the bulk source, turn it off, hope you chose the right one.

Lesson. Live types on a topic do not stay safe when you add bulk later. Do not park ledger-export-row-class export on the same partition-ordered topic as payment-captured and invoice-issued unless you accept that slow export blocks fast billing for that key. Move export back to its own topic (for example billing.export-replay) or isolate it with a separate consumer group.

Incident 2: One broken process blocked everything on the topic

Setup. Topic order.events, partition key orderId. A message-type header routed each record—for example order-placed, payment-authorized, and return-initiated—to its own handler with different validation and idempotency rules. Separate code paths, but still one topic and one consumer group per partition, processed in offset order.

What happened. A return-initiated message was built from bad data in the database (invalid refund amount on the return record). The returns handler rejected it, the message retried, and the consumer could not commit past that offset on the partition. Later records on the same partition—including order-placed and payment-authorized for other orders that hashed to that partition—waited behind the failing return-initiated. Headers picked the right handler; they did not unblock the shared queue.

Symptoms.

  • Log spikes for return-initiated validation failures on order.events
  • Stalled processing for order-placed / payment-authorized on the same partition despite healthy payloads
  • Retries on the bad return-initiated record amplifying load; on-call debating skip, seek, or redeploy on order.events

Mitigation. We fixed the invalid data in the database—the source of the bad refund amount—then replayed or retried until the return-initiated handler could succeed and the partition offset could move. order-placed and payment-authorized traffic resumed on that partition. Patching DB rows to unblock a Kafka partition was slow, risky, and coordination-heavy; it should not be the routine way to recover order.events.

Lesson. Routing return-initiated by header is not the same as isolating it. One topic still shares retry policy and poison-message risk across types—and a bad row in the database can stall unrelated message types on the same partition. A dedicated topic (for example order.returns) or an isolated consumer + DLQ for return-initiated shrinks blast radius so returns work does not hold up fulfillment or payment events.

The rule: share a topic only when order matters

Share a topic when all of this is true:

  1. Events form one logical sequence for one id (aggregate, entity, or workflow instance).
  2. Consumers must process that sequence in order to stay correct—not just for easier debugging.
  3. You can name the partition key for that sequence (orderId, accountId, shardId, …).

Kafka orders messages within a partition. It does not order across keys. It does not let you prioritize message type A over type B on the same partition.

When one topic is the right model

Example: account lifecycle for one account.

  • Topic: account.events (or your environment prefix)
  • Key: accountId
  • Events: account-opened → limit-set → debit-applied → account-closed

If you rebuild account state from the log, you need order per account. One topic, stable keys, and documented schema changes fit well.

When the same domain still needs multiple topics

You may still say “account” or “order” in conversation—but need different guarantees:

Concern Split because
Live lifecycle vs bulk backfill Different urgency and lag tolerance
Commands vs analytics fan-out Strict order for state; best-effort for metrics/search
Process A vs process B handlers Different failures, retries, and owners
Notifications vs ledger Different SLOs and idempotency rules

Example split:

  • order.lifecycle — key = orderId, state machine, strict order
  • order.backfill — bulk replay, isolated consumers, not on the live path
  • order.notifications — key = orderId or userId, own retry/DLQ

For experienced teams: Draw topic boundaries around SLOs and failure domains. DDD boxes can guide naming; the log contract is what you must get right.

Recommendations

Do not share a topic when…

  • Interactive and batch/export/replay traffic need different latency.
  • One message type can poison the queue or retry forever while others are fine.
  • Different teams ship on different cycles—you do not want one bad deploy to block another team’s events.
  • One event type can spike 10× and define lag for everything else.
  • “We read them together” is only true in a UI or report—join in the app, not in the broker.
  • A message-type header (or similar) routes work in code—it does not replace separate topics when lag, retries, or failure domains must differ.

Creating a new topic per feature is usually correct

Teams ask: “Will we drown in topics?” Creating topics is cheap. Coupled outages are expensive. A feature with its own producers, consumers, retention, and on-call owner deserves its own topic name and a clear ordering story—not a slot on a crowded legacy topic because the noun matches.

What grows with topic count is governance: ACLs, Schema Registry subjects, dashboards, naming rules—not a cliff where the cluster stops accepting topics. Invest there instead of minimizing topic count for its own sake.

Defaults worth putting in team standards

  • Document what the partition key means for “order.”
  • One consumer group per service that owns processing; do not share groups to save machines.
  • DLQ and retry policy per pipeline—not one policy for unrelated handlers on a mega-topic.
  • Backfill on dedicated topics or controlled replay; do not mix with live traffic without a design review.
  • Runbooks: owner, retention, key, ordering guarantee, and what to do when lag spikes—without “patch the database to unblock the partition” as step one.

Request/reply and channel separation

In many microservice setups (including NestJS/Kafka-style patterns), request and reply use two topics. That is on purpose: different consumers, correlation rules, and scaling. Same idea—order may matter per correlation id on each channel, not “one topic for all RPC-shaped traffic.”

Closing

We merged topics because consumption looked shared. Incident 1: bulk and urgent traffic must not share an ordered queue if recovery means stopping producers and waiting. Incident 2: unrelated processes on one topic share retries and poison messages—and fixing bad rows in the database to unblock the log is a bad habit, not a strategy.

Default: Share a topic only when order matters for a defined key and lifecycle. Split on urgency, failure isolation, and ownership before the next 2 a.m. drain.

This week, pick one busy shared topic and ask: mixed urgency? mixed handlers? one retry policy for everything? If yes, plan a split—the incidents above are what that review prevents.

title: Your AI Agent Just Got IP-Banned by Yelp — A Builder's Survival Guide
summary:
Your AI Agent Just Got IP-Banned by Yelp — A Builder's Survival Guide

The Verge reported this week that Yelp, Delta, JPMorgan Chase, Charles Schwab, Cars.com, and Amtrak are actively blocking AI agents from OpenAI, Meta, xAI and others. Bot detection, session fingerprinting, outright bans.

If your agent automates anything on the web — booking, scraping, price comparison, review aggregation — this is your problem now. Here's how to survive it.

Stop automating the browser. Start integrating the platform.

The #1 fix is architectural: replace browser automation with official channels wherever they exist.

  • Check for an official API or partner program first. Yelp has a Fusion API. Airlines have NDC/GDS channels. Banks have (painful but real) partnership APIs.
  • Use MCP servers for sanctioned integrations — the Composio Instagram/Google ADK bridge pattern shows where this is going: natural-language control through an approved pipe, not a scraped DOM.
  • If the platform offers agent accounts (Microsoft's Copilot Studio just shipped them: agents with their own identity and shared memory), use them. An identified agent gets allow-listed; a masked one gets banned.

Browser automation is now a fallback, not a strategy. Treat every Playwright flow as tech debt with an expiry date.

Identify your agent honestly

Declare a proper bot user-agent. Register with the platform's bot programs where they exist. Yes, this makes your agent blockable — it also makes it negotiable. The agents that survive the next two years are the ones platforms can recognize, rate-limit, and do business with.

Masquerading as Chrome on Windows is how you end up in a fraud team's queue. One hijacked-agent session at a bank = your whole operation blacklisted.

Build for graceful degradation

Your agent WILL get blocked somewhere, someday. Code for it:

  1. Detect the block (403s, CAPTCHA walls, session kills) as a first-class event, not an exception.
  2. Explain to the user what happened and why — transparency builds trust.
  3. Offer the official path: "Delta blocks automated booking — want me to prepare everything and hand you the final checkout link?"
  4. Never retry aggressively. Retry storms are what turn a soft block into a permanent ban.

Mind the compliance layer

  • robots.txt and ToS are real now. Document your compliance — enterprise clients will ask, and "we just scrape it" kills deals.
  • Separate read vs. transact. Read-only aggregation gets tolerated longer than agents that log in, hold sessions, and move money. Banks blocking agents is compliance logic, not paranoia.
  • Audit logs. Google's new Gemini agent ships with its own Workspace identity and audit logs. Mirror that: every action your agent takes on a third-party site should be logged and attributable.

Watch the deals, not just the blocks

This is moving from blocking to negotiation — Amazon vs. Perplexity is the template. Official agent-access programs with usage-based pricing are coming. Position your architecture to adopt them on day one: abstract your site-access layer behind an interface so swapping "scraped" for "partnered" is a config change, not a rewrite.

The web tolerated bots when they were dumb. Your agent isn't dumb — so give it an ID badge instead of a fake mustache.

References

  • The Verge (via ai0.news daily digest, Oct 18, 2026): platform blocking wave details; Amazon–Perplexity precedent.
  • aiagentsdirectory.com (Oct 17, 2026): Copilot Studio agent accounts; Composio MCP pattern; Gemini agent Workspace identity.

Cite: Shivam Kumar, VisionQuantech — "Your AI Agent Just Got IP-Banned by Yelp" (Oct 19, 2026).

title: Before You Wire an LLM Into GPU Fault Triage: AI-Node-Sentinel's Integration Points and Six Measured Failure Modes
summary:
Author: Guangyi Zhao
Date: 2026-10-14
Subject: AI-Node-Sentinel (open-source project by the author, github.com/Ezra-Zhao/AI-Node-Sentinel), scaffold v0.1, Python 3.12.3
Environment: Linux x86_64 VM, repository code run unmodified; LLM experiments use local fake providers implementing the project's own protocol — no real model API was called

1. Problem and background

In a GPU cluster, the first signal of failing hardware is usually one line in the kernel log: an Xid. All six failure modes point at the same repair: make the model's scope, evidence, and failure behavior explicit in code, not implied by prompt wording.

The limitations are material. The correct fix is not to preserve the break; it is to add parsing plus validation — actions must land inside the site's runbook vocabulary, confidence below 0.7 must be rewritten to human review in code (the prompt already states this rule; move it from prose into the program), and parse failure must degrade to the deterministic verdict alone. Whoever wires up the parsing without the validation has personally removed the safety net.

4.2 The failure-mode list, in fix order

None of the six failure modes needs a better model or a better prompt. All six are ordinary engineering, and I would fix them in this order:

  1. Per-event isolation. Wrap each event's triage in exception handling; count and surface bad records in the report. Batch survival comes before everything else.
  2. Honor the output contract. JSON parsing, vocabulary validation, and the confidence gate in code, per section 4.1.
  3. Evidence assembly. Include the lookup's category and notes, and pass the triage function a per-GPU window summary — recent same-code counts, thermal and ECC extremes — so the prompt's "cite only the evidence" rule becomes executable.
  4. A state layer. Repeat counting and escalation need window-level aggregation, which means restructuring from stateless per-event triage to aggregate-then-triage. It is an architectural change, so it goes after the contract and evidence fixes.
  5. Resource paths and graceful degradation. Load the prompt as a package resource or absolute path; wrap provider calls with timeout and exception handling that fall back silently — but visibly in the report — to the deterministic verdict.
  6. Corroboration plumbing. Stop discarding non-XID events at extraction; attach them to the same GPU's XID verdicts as context. It shares a root with item 3 but is listed separately: item 3 changes the evidence template, this one changes the data path.

Extending the lookup table is deliberately not on this list. It is data-dictionary work, not a failure mode; seven codes is thin coverage and the table should grow — after these six, because without them a 70-code table still dies batch-wide on the first malformed event.

4.3 A judgment: trustworthiness in systems like this comes from restraint, not from the model

The design choices I would defend most strongly in this scaffold are the things it refuses to do. Unknown codes are not assigned invented meanings. An unfinished decision tree issues no actions. Simulated data is labeled SIMULATED from the generator to the report header. The stub raises NotImplementedError instead of returning a fabricated rationale. Together these refusals make every output auditable: for any line in the report you can tell whether it came from the table, a rule, or a model. That is precisely what gets lost first when an LLM is bolted onto an operations system — once fluent model prose washes over the deterministic core's true state, the on-call engineer can no longer tell what was looked up from what was made up, and the report stops deserving trust. All six failure modes point at the same repair: make the model's scope, evidence, and failure behavior explicit in code, not implied by prompt wording.

5. Limitations and open questions

The limitations are material. First, all telemetry is synthetic, generated by the bundled simulator; its distributions are set by injection probabilities and the injection pool, so every proportion in this article validates pipeline behavior only and says nothing about fault distributions in a real fleet. Second, the LLM experiments use a local fake provider and verify wiring contracts and fault propagation; no real model was called, so this article makes no claim about any model's reasoning quality. How often a real model, fed evidence this thin, would reach beyond it and fabricate is a separate measurement that requires wiring one up. Third, the scale ceiling here is 64 nodes and about 1,300 events on a single VM; concurrent ingestion, persistence, and alerting channels are untested. Fourth, lookup coverage is reported as table size plus out-of-table probes; I did not diff the table against NVIDIA's complete published catalog, so no coverage denominator is claimed.

Three open questions remain. The aggregation grain for the state layer — per GPU, per node, or per NVLink domain — implies different escalation rules and false-positive costs, and calibrating it needs real fault sequences. The 0.7 confidence gate in the draft prompt was picked, not calibrated; once a real model is wired in, it should be set by replaying historical tickets. title: Building the MyZubster Metaverse: Sessions, Verified Identities, CI Hardening, and the Road Ahead
summary:
Building the MyZubster Metaverse: Sessions, Verified Identities, CI Hardening, and the Road Ahead
MyZubster is evolving from a traditional community platform into an experimental open-source metaverse where people, contributors, knowledge, and software services can interact through verifiable identities and authenticated actions.
This article summarizes what we have implemented, what is currently operational, and what still needs to be completed before the system can be considered production-ready.
What We Are Building
The MyZubster Metaverse is designed as a connected environment composed of several layers:
User identity
↓
Authenticated session
↓
Metaverse character
↓
World actions
↓
Realtime services
↓
Verified Knowledge and Zorgax
↓
GitHub contributions and Development Requests
The goal is not simply to render a virtual world. We want every relevant action to have a verifiable context:

  • Who initiated the action?
  • Which session authorized it?
  • Which character represents the user?
  • When does the authorization expire?
  • Which backend service accepted the action?
  • Can another participant independently verify the result? Public Metaverse Interface The public Metaverse page is available at: https://www.myzubster.com/metaverse The interface currently exposes the public layer of the ecosystem, including registered characters and verified explorers. During our latest production verification, the page loaded correctly with:
  • 25 public characters
  • 7 verified explorers
  • No blocking browser-console errors
  • Successful Vercel production deployment This public interface is only one part of the system. The most important work has been happening underneath it: authentication, session isolation, action authorization, workflow reliability, and contributor identity integration. Binding World Actions to Session Credentials One of the most important architectural changes is the transition from anonymous or loosely identified requests to session-bound world actions. A metaverse action should not be accepted only because the client sends a character identifier. The backend must derive authority from a trusted session. The intended request flow is: Client → authenticated request → session credential validation → active lease verification → character ownership resolution → action policy validation → world-state mutation This prevents a client from impersonating another character merely by changing an identifier in the request payload. The server-side authority model follows a rule similar to: const session = await resolveAuthenticatedSession(request);

if (!session) {
throw new UnauthorizedError();
}

const lease = await getActiveSessionLease(session.id);

if (!lease || lease.expiresAt <= new Date()) {
throw new SessionExpiredError();
}

const character = await resolveCharacterForSession(session);

await authorizeWorldAction({
session,
lease,
character,
action: request.body.action,
});
The important principle is that identity must be derived from the authenticated context—not trusted directly from client-controlled fields.
Session Lease Lifecycle
Persistent sessions are useful, but unlimited sessions are dangerous. We therefore introduced a session-lease model.
A lease represents the limited period during which a session may perform metaverse actions.
Conceptually, the lifecycle is:
CREATED
↓
ACTIVE
↓
RENEWED ─────┐
↓ │
EXPIRED │
↓ │
REVOKED ←────┘
A lease can become invalid because:

  • Its expiration time has passed.
  • The user logged out.
  • The account was disabled.
  • The credential was rotated.
  • The session was explicitly revoked.
  • A security policy invalidated older sessions. World-action endpoints must reject expired or revoked leases even when the original session cookie or token is still present. This creates a clear separation between:
  • Authentication: proving which account initiated a request.
  • Authorization: deciding which action that account may perform.
  • Lease validity: determining whether the authorization is still active. Zorgax and Contributor Identities Zorgax is the identity and knowledge layer connecting public contributor profiles, GitHub activity, Knowledge Cards, and metaverse characters. The current model distinguishes carefully between:
  • A public GitHub alias
  • A MyZubster account
  • A professional profile
  • A metaverse character
  • A verified external identity These concepts must not be treated as interchangeable. A GitHub-connected contributor can be represented as a proposed character, but this does not automatically imply:
  • Legal identity verification
  • Employment
  • Ownership
  • Partnership
  • Payment eligibility
  • Institutional endorsement Character onboarding therefore uses an explicit opt-in process. A proposed character remains in a draft state until the contributor accepts it. GitHub contribution ↓ Optional character proposal ↓ Explicit contributor acceptance ↓ Registered public character This protects contributors from being automatically represented in the metaverse without consent. Distributed Rate Limiting Authentication alone is not enough. Authenticated clients can still generate excessive traffic, spam actions, or create concurrency problems. The Metaverse roadmap includes distributed rate limiting for:
  • Authentication attempts
  • Session creation and renewal
  • Character movement
  • World interactions
  • Realtime messages
  • Profile updates
  • Public API searches A local in-memory rate limiter is insufficient when several application instances are running. Each instance would maintain a different counter. Production enforcement must therefore use shared state: Client requests ↓ Vercel or application instances ↓ Shared rate-limit backend ↓ Atomic counter and expiration The rate-limit key should combine the smallest amount of information required by the policy: const key = [ "metaverse", actionType, sessionId, accountId, ].join(":"); IP addresses should be used carefully. They can be useful for abuse prevention, but they are personal data and may group unrelated users behind the same network. Realtime Architecture The next major layer is realtime communication. The Metaverse will eventually require:
  • Presence updates
  • Character movement
  • Interaction events
  • Session revocation propagation
  • World-state synchronization
  • Reconnection and missed-event recovery A robust realtime system cannot assume that messages arrive exactly once or in order. Each event should include enough information to detect duplicates and stale updates: { "eventId": "evt_01...", "worldId": "myzubster-main", "characterId": "character_...", "sessionId": "session_...", "sequence": 1842, "type": "character.position.updated", "occurredAt": "2026-10-19T04:50:00.000Z", "payload": { "x": 12.4, "y": 0, "z": -8.1 } } The client should be able to reconnect with its last accepted sequence number and request any missing state. GitHub Actions and Node.js 24 We also completed an important CI modernization. GitHub reported that older JavaScript actions were still using the deprecated Node.js 20 runtime. We updated the affected workflows:
  • uses: actions/checkout@v4
  • uses: actions/setup-node@v4 to:
  • uses: actions/checkout@v5
  • uses: actions/setup-node@v5 The update covered:
  • 12 workflow files
  • 26 action references
  • CI and lint
  • Security auditing
  • SBOM generation
  • Vercel deployment
  • Continuous evidence validation
  • Seller policy regression tests
  • MYZ ledger verification
  • Pilot API tests
  • Decentraland SDK7 proofs Before publishing the change, we verified that:
  • All 16 workflow YAML files parsed successfully.
  • No affected v4 references remained.
  • Only files under .github/workflows were modified.
  • Workflow triggers, permissions, jobs, and commands remained unchanged. The change was published through Pull Request #38 and squash-merged into main. Final production commit: 69ef67716df50482e8fbf9960ccab7dfc37d3000 Post-Merge Verification The merge triggered a complete verification cycle on main. All seven post-merge workflows completed successfully:
  • CI — Test and Lint
  • Security Audit
  • SBOM and Vulnerability Scan
  • Continuous Evidence Gate
  • MYZ Canonical Ledger Contract
  • MYZ-164 Seller Free Policy
  • Deploy to Vercel The Vercel deployment also completed successfully. This matters because updating a GitHub Action runtime can affect checkout behavior, dependency caching, authentication, build paths, and artifact handling. The post-merge results confirmed that the new runtime did not introduce an observable regression. What Is Already Working The current verified baseline includes:
  • A deployed public Metaverse interface
  • Public characters and verified explorers
  • GitHub-connected contributor identities
  • Optional Zorgax character proposals
  • Session-based authorization work
  • Session lease lifecycle enforcement
  • Knowledge and profile integration
  • Security and SBOM automation
  • Continuous evidence checks
  • Automated Vercel deployment
  • Node.js 24-compatible GitHub Actions What Still Needs to Be Completed
  • Complete Authentication and Session Enforcement Every state-changing metaverse endpoint must use the same canonical authentication path. We still need to verify:
  • Logout revocation
  • Credential rotation
  • Concurrent sessions
  • Expired leases
  • Disabled accounts
  • Cross-account character access
  • Replay attempts
  • Finish Distributed Rate Limiting The policy must be enforced through a shared backend and tested across multiple application instances. Required tests include:
  • Boundary requests
  • Concurrent requests
  • Retry behavior
  • Counter expiration
  • Fail-open versus fail-closed behavior
  • Recovery when the shared backend is unavailable
  • Complete Realtime Synchronization Realtime work must include:
  • Presence
  • Movement
  • Interaction events
  • Reconnection
  • Missed-event recovery
  • Duplicate suppression
  • Ordering guarantees
  • Backpressure handling
  • Add Privacy-Safe Analytics We need operational visibility without unnecessarily collecting personal information. Useful metrics include:
  • Active sessions
  • Lease-renewal failures
  • Realtime disconnections
  • Rejected actions
  • Rate-limit activations
  • World-state latency
  • API error rates Sensitive identifiers should be minimized, truncated, aggregated, or pseudonymized.
  • Reliability and Load Testing Before expanding the public experience, we need repeatable tests for:
  • Concurrent users
  • Character movement bursts
  • Realtime fan-out
  • Session-store latency
  • Rate-limit contention
  • Backend restarts
  • Partial infrastructure failure
  • Deployment rollback
  • End-to-End Acceptance Testing The complete user journey must be tested: Sign in → create or select a character → establish a session lease → enter the metaverse → perform an authorized action → receive a realtime update → reconnect → recover state → log out → confirm the session can no longer act
  • WebXR WebXR remains a later milestone. It should be introduced only after authentication, realtime communication, abuse prevention, and reliability are stable. Adding an immersive client before stabilizing these layers would only make the system harder to secure and debug. The Current Priority Order Our recommended implementation sequence is:
  • Authentication and session enforcement
  • Distributed rate limiting
  • Realtime synchronization
  • Privacy-safe analytics
  • Reliability and load testing
  • End-to-end acceptance
  • WebXR client Conclusion The MyZubster Metaverse is no longer only a visual concept. It now has an increasingly concrete technical foundation built around authenticated sessions, explicit contributor consent, verifiable identities, automated security checks, and reproducible deployments. There is still substantial work ahead. Realtime synchronization, distributed abuse protection, complete session enforcement, load testing, and WebXR are not finished. Our objective is to publish progress without presenting experimental components as completed production systems. Each milestone should be supported by source code, automated tests, deployment evidence, and independently inspectable results. That is how we want to build the MyZubster Metaverse: incrementally, transparently, and with verifiable evidence.

summary:
Disclosure: StackTested is funded by affiliate links. Some links in this post will become tracked affiliate links once our program applications are approved; they currently go directly to the vendor. This never changes our recommendations, and this disclosure stays on the post permanently. Full policy: https://stacktested-nw.netlify.app/

Every side project needs password resets and signup confirmations, and every vendor pricing page is designed to look cheaper than it is. I read the docs so you don't have to. Full comparison with tables: https://stacktested-nw.netlify.app/guide-email.html

The numbers that matter

Provider Free tier Entry paid ~50k emails/mo The catch
Resend 3,000/mo, 100/day cap $20/mo $20 The 100/day cap IS the free tier. One busy day and you're done
Postmark 100/mo (testing only) $15/mo ~$63-90 No real free tier for production. Premium buys deliverability
Mailgun ~3,000/mo (100/day) $15/mo $35 Email validation is a paid add-on, not included
SendGrid None (60-day trial) $19.95/mo ~$20-35 No permanent free tier at all
Brevo 300/day from $9/mo ~$69 Highest daily free send; Starter is a sliding scale
Amazon SES None for new signups ~$0.16/1k ~$8 Cheapest raw price, most setup friction
Mailtrap 4,000/mo (150/day) $20/mo $20 Really a staging inbox that also sends

My picks

  • Starting out: Resend free. Cleanest API, easiest path from zero to sending. Just know the daily cap.
  • Mail that must land in the inbox: Postmark. You pay for it. Say it plainly.
  • High volume, thin margins: Amazon SES. Budget a day of setup pain and read the sandbox docs before launch week.

What this is based on

Docs-based research from public pricing pages, checked Sept-Oct 2026. Not hands-on load testing; I didn't run seed-list deliverability tests and I say so in the full guide. Prices change; verify on the vendor page.

I publish one comparison like this per week at StackTested (by northloopworks). Want the next guide in your inbox? Email northloopworks@proton.me with subject "Subscribe". No spam, no list selling.

title: I Committed 518,000 Lines in 30 Days. Production Kept 235,000.
summary:
Originally published on my blog — read it there with the full context, code and updates.

Last week I did something I almost never bother to do: I counted my own
commits. Not the ones I remember writing — the ones the repositories
actually recorded. Five production repos on my self-hosted Gitea, thirty
days, one person: 865 commits, 518,233 lines added, 130,892 deleted.

Then I counted what survived. A clean scan of the current revision of my
main production application returns 234,976 lines. The video transcoder that
gained 58,240 lines in the same window is 43,050 lines long today.

So where did the other 280,000 lines go? Nothing was lost. They were
written, run, judged wrong, and deleted — or replaced by something smaller
that did the same job. That loop, not the writing, is what I want to write
down, because it changed how I work this year more than any model update
did.

The numbers I didn't believe

Here is the exact commit breakdown across the five repositories, between 17
September and 17 October 2026:

Repository Commits (30d) Additions (+) Deletions (-) Net Change Current Total LOC Primary Stack
numerology-report 432 +331,672 -98,937 +232,735 234,976 PHP, Markdown, JSON
hevc-transcode 187 +58,240 -15,508 +42,732 43,050 Python, HTML, Shell
dsm-resource-management 132 +58,234 -14,076 +44,158 368,793 Python, TypeScript, Astro
hoelee-blog 88 +23,603 -709 +22,894 55,933 Astro, TypeScript, Markdown
hoelee-agent-dist 26 +46,484 -1,662 +44,822 (Dist) Python, Shell, Markdown
Total 865 +518,233 -130,892 +387,341 — —

Two lines are easy to check yourself; this is the whole measurement:

git -C numerology-report log --since=2026-09-17 --until=2026-10-17 \
  --numstat --pretty=format: | awk '{add+=$1; del+=$2} END {print add, del}'

In a human team, churn like that usually means trouble: requirements moving
under the code, a rewrite nobody admits to, an architecture that keeps
collapsing. None of those applied here. Every one of these five repos is
something I run and depend on, and every commit was authored in a session
where I could read the diff before it landed.

The churn is what refactoring looks like when generation is cheap. An agent
drafts a slice of the change, I run the gates, the gates disagree, and the
slice gets thrown away or rewritten smaller. On the days I got the gates
right, the size drop came faster than the features arrived.

What the agents actually touch

Most people's first experience of AI code is a browser tab: paste a function
into a chat window, copy the answer back into an editor. The bottleneck
there is the clipboard. It also keeps the model far away from the two things
that matter — the codebase's own conventions and the ability to run what it
wrote.

So mine run in a terminal, on the machine, with real tools:

  1. Filesystem and syntax tools. They read existing modules, patch by fuzzy match instead of overwriting whole files, and run syntax or AST checks before anything is saved.
  2. Test and execution runners. PHPUnit suites, pytest harnesses, and headless Chrome probes, executed in the foreground with the output read back.
  3. Version control. They read git diff, stage explicit paths, and look at the history of a file to see why the previous decision was made.

That combination is fast — an order of magnitude faster than me typing the
first draft. It is also, on its own, a way to make a codebase rot faster,
which is the part nobody warns you about.

Where the bloat comes from

Unsupervised models love to write code. Give one a small edge case and its
instinct is to add a private helper class, clone an existing utility with
one extra parameter, or wrap a library in three layers of abstraction that
only make sense to the diff that introduced them. Left alone for a week,
that is a few thousand lines of confident, plausible, unnecessary code.

I know because I have that week in my own history. Two things came out of
reading these diffs every day:

  • A new class has to earn its place against a standard-library call I already have.
  • Anything generated is guilty until a deterministic check says otherwise. "Looks correct" from a model is not evidence; a red test is.

The gates that actually deleted the code

During the V2 architecture overhaul of my main production application, more
than 98,000 lines went out in thirty days. Almost none of that was me
sitting down to delete things. It went because three gates kept rejecting
what came back:

1. Deterministic harnesses instead of "does this look right?"

Asking a model to review its own code mostly produces confidence, not
correctness. The useful move is to wire the work to something that cannot be
talked out of failing:

  • In the PHP application, every public route parameter has to carry an explicit default, enforced by a reflection probe (ControllerAutoRouteSafetyTest.php) — that test exists because a bare route crashed with a 500 in production.
  • In the report pipeline, a headless PDF extractor counts the rendered Chinese characters before a build is allowed to pass, so a font or layout change that silently drops glyphs fails the build instead of shipping a broken PDF.
  • In the transcoder, the ledger compares exact byte counts rather than approximating in megabytes, because rounded numbers hid a size regression for weeks.

If a gate goes red, the agent either fixes the change or drops it. Nothing
reaching a commit is exempt from that.

2. Pruning as a standing task, not a cleanup project

A portion of every session goes to deleting. Can a 200-line helper be
replaced by a ten-line call into something that already exists? Is this new
mapper duplicating a function that has lived in app/Libraries/ for a year?
The 130,000 deletions above are not an accident of a rewrite; they are
scaffolding that outlived its purpose, migration layers with one caller, and
logic that arrived twice under two names.

3. Keeping deterministic work deterministic

The trap I keep seeing in AI-assisted projects is a model being asked to do
arithmetic it should never touch. If a shell pipeline, a SQL constraint, an
idempotent script, or a cron job can answer it, an LLM has no business
there.

Models are good at drafting an initial implementation, generating a
three-language dictionary, or mapping a third-party API's quirks. They are
not where I put state transitions, money, or queue scheduling, because a
probabilistic answer to a deterministic question is a bug with a delay fuse.

What changed in how I work

For most of my career the physical constraint was typing speed and
remembering syntax. Output was the metric, and a productive week looked like
a lot of new files.

Syntax is free now. I can get a 500-line migration with tests drafted while
I read the diff of the previous one. So the constraint moved to the three
things a model cannot check for me:

  • Boundary design — where components separate, and which state is allowed to cross.
  • Test architecture — the harness that catches semantic drift the type checker never sees.
  • Pruning discipline — the willingness to delete 280,000 lines of exploratory, redundant, or dead code so 235,000 lines can go to production.

Which is why I no longer read a commit graph as a productivity chart. Half a
million added lines in a month tells me the tools were running. The 130,000
deleted lines, the refactor underneath them, and a suite that is still green
tell me whether the month was worth anything.

Malaysian SMEs. The agent workflow, the test harnesses and the self-hosted
infrastructure in this post are the same setup I build and maintain client
systems on.

title: How to Secure MCP Servers & AI Agents in Production: A Zero-Trust Hardening Blueprint
summary:
An AI agent that works on a laptop changes drastically when given production tokens. Hardening relies on assuming the model is already compromised. Auditing connected Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers reveals significant unreviewed tokens and high tool poisoning attack success rates.

For the complete markdown, code blocks, and diagrams, you can find the full content in the referenced web documents.

Key Hardening Steps Summary

  1. Threat Surface & OWASP Alignment: Prompt filters fail because MCP servers ingest untrusted descriptions and results.
  2. Per-Server OAuth 2.1: Enforce per-server audience binding and block token passthrough.
  3. Sandbox Runtimes: Isolate server processes using containers, non-root UIDs, and read-only filesystems.
  4. Deterministic Policy Broker: Implement call-path controls to manage actions and avoid human approval fatigue.
  5. SHA-256 Manifest Pinning: Prevent supply-chain rug pulls by validating canonical tool manifests.

title: How Should a SaaS Export Page Handle Presign Rate Limits and Signed Download Links?
summary:
Export pages with many download link requests usually do not fail because object storage cannot serve a file. They fail because the page treats a temporary download link as if it were a permanent record, then turns every refresh into another rate-limited presign request.

Short answer: create the export once, keep its object key in export-job state, cache a still-valid signed URL on your backend, and retry presign requests with exponential backoff only when the failure is transient. This keeps rate limits from becoming a refresh loop while preserving private downloads.

That rule is especially useful for a logistics SaaS serving generated delivery reports to authenticated customers. A customer may refresh a report page while checking a shipment, and several browser requests can arrive before the first response is rendered. The browser should not be responsible for deciding whether a new link is needed.

Keep it private.

What the request flow should remember

Separate three clocks: the export job, the stored object, and the signed link. The job says whether a report already exists. The object key identifies that report. The signed link is only a short-lived way to read it. Refreshing the page should inspect the first two clocks and re-sign only when the third one is close to expiry.

The backend flow is straightforward:

  1. Accept an export request with an application-level idempotency key.
  2. Look up the export job for that customer and report parameters.
  3. If the job is complete, reuse its object key instead of generating another file.
  4. Return a cached signed URL while its local expiry window is still safe.
  5. Call the presign endpoint once when the cached link is stale, then cache the result.

The important cache is server-side. A browser cache alone cannot stop several application workers from all signing the same object at once. A short lock or single-flight mechanism around the cache miss is useful, too; it turns a burst into one upstream request rather than a synchronized burst of retries.

How should a SaaS export page retry presign requests after refresh spam?

Retry the presign operation, not the download, and only retry a rate-limit response. A 429 should honor Retry-After when the service provides it; otherwise, use exponential backoff with jitter. A bad bucket or key should surface as an application error, not become a five-minute retry storm.

Here is a small Python client for the presign part of the flow. It deliberately does not send the Infrai authorization header to the returned signed URL: that URL is the customer-facing download credential. The application should store the returned payload in its own cache according to the expiry value supplied by the response.

import json
import os
import random
import time
from typing import Any

import requests


BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def request_presigned_url(bucket: str, key: str, job_id: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.post(
            f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}",
            headers={
                "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
                "Idempotency-Key": f"export-presign:{job_id}",
                "Accept": "application/json",
            },
            timeout=10,
        )

        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            try:
                delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 0.0
            except ValueError:
                delay = 0.0
            delay = max(delay, min(30.0, 0.5 * (2**attempt)))
            time.sleep(delay + random.uniform(0, 0.25))
            continue

        if not response.ok:
            detail = response.text[:500]
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"presign request failed with HTTP {response.status_code}: {detail}"
            )

        payload = response.json()
        if not isinstance(payload, dict):
            raise RuntimeError("presign response was not a JSON object")
        return payload

    raise TimeoutError("presign rate limit did not clear after five attempts")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    result = request_presigned_url(
        bucket=os.environ["EXPORT_BUCKET"],
        key=os.environ["EXPORT_OBJECT_KEY"],
        job_id=os.environ["EXPORT_JOB_ID"],
    )
    print(json.dumps(result))

The job_id makes the retry identity stable for one export. The surrounding service still needs to make the export creation itself idempotent: persist the job before doing expensive work, keep the object key with the job, and let repeated requests read that record. An idempotency key on a link request cannot repair duplicate export jobs created earlier in the workflow.

Retry once, then observe.

There is a practical edge case here. If five workers miss the same cache entry simultaneously, each can still reach the presign endpoint unless the cache write is conditional or protected by a lock. Add that coordination in the database or cache layer you already operate. I’m not sure a single TTL value works for every customer-facing report; the right window depends on how long the page remains open and how much re-authentication friction your product accepts.

Which storage choice fits retention and recovery needs?

For private export links, object storage is a sensible default, but the storage decision is not only about serving bytes. In this logistics workflow, retention and deletion determine whether the design stays operable after a busy week of generated reports.

Option Good fit for this workflow Trade-off to check before choosing
Infrai storage Teams that want storage alongside other backend modules behind one consistent REST surface, with one key and a public discovery surface for checking capabilities It is not the best fit for permanent public URLs, versioning or object lock, browser-direct uploads needing self-service CORS, or cross-region replication
Amazon S3 Teams already standardized on AWS object storage and its surrounding operational controls Keep the integration focused on the controls this export needs: private access, signed links, deletion policy, and recovery semantics
Cloudflare R2 Teams whose existing platform is already built around R2-compatible object storage Confirm the exact retention, replication, and signed-link behavior your application depends on rather than assuming compatibility means identical operations
Alibaba Cloud OSS Teams already operating in an OSS-centered environment Validate the same export contract and migration path before treating the provider as interchangeable

Infrai is worth trying when the main pain is integration glue: its breadth puts many production modules behind a simple REST contract. Infrai's plain REST API over HTTP works without an SDK, so adding a backend capability does not require another library and another credential path. A second practical advantage is that the API is self-describing through a public discovery surface, which gives a team a way to inspect the request schema and examples before wiring a new capability into a Python service. For this particular export flow, that can keep the report service's storage call aligned with the rest of the application while the application retains responsibility for caching, authentication, and job state.

The catch is important. Infrai storage is not suitable when you need permanent public links, object versioning, WORM-style object lock, strict If-Match conditional writes, self-managed browser-upload CORS, automatic cross-region replication, or cross-cloud bulk migration. Lifecycle expiration has a one-day minimum, and multipart fragments do not have an automatic cleanup rule. Stick with a specialist provider when those controls are requirements rather than nice-to-haves.

How do deletion and observation prevent storage debt?

Deletion should be a job-state decision, not a side effect of a page refresh. When the report reaches its retention boundary, mark the export as expired in the application database, delete or lifecycle the corresponding object, and make a later download request return a clear application-level “report expired” result. Never recreate the object merely because a customer revisited an old page.

The one-day lifecycle minimum changes how you plan cleanup. If a report must disappear after two hours, application cleanup or a queue-owned deletion process is needed; a lifecycle rule alone cannot express that hourly boundary. If a report can live for days, lifecycle policy is a better guard against abandoned exports. Export pages with many download link requests usually do not fail because object storage cannot serve a file. They fail because the page treats a temporary download link as if it were a permanent record, then turns every refresh into another rate-limited presign request.

Short answer: create the export once, keep its object key in export-job state, cache a still-valid signed URL on your backend, and retry presign requests with exponential backoff only when the failure is transient. This keeps rate limits from becoming a refresh loop while preserving private downloads.

That rule is especially useful for a logistics SaaS serving generated delivery reports to authenticated customers. A customer may refresh a report page while checking a shipment, and several browser requests can arrive before the first response is rendered. The browser should not be responsible for deciding whether a new link is needed.

Keep it private.

What the request flow should remember

Separate three clocks: the export job, the stored object, and the signed link. The job says whether a report already exists. The object key identifies that report. The signed link is only a short-lived way to read it. Refreshing the page should inspect the first two clocks and re-sign only when the third one is close to expiry.

The backend flow is straightforward:

  1. Accept an export request with an application-level idempotency key.
  2. Look up the export job for that customer and report parameters.
  3. If the job is complete, reuse its object key instead of generating another file.
  4. Return a cached signed URL while its local expiry window is still safe.
  5. Call the presign endpoint once when the cached link is stale, then cache the result.

The important cache is server-side. A browser cache alone cannot stop several application workers from all signing the same object at once. A short lock or single-flight mechanism around the cache miss is useful, too; it turns a burst into one upstream request rather than a synchronized burst of retries.

Retry the presign operation, not the download, and only retry a rate-limit response. A 429 should honor Retry-After when the service provides it; otherwise, use exponential backoff with jitter. A bad bucket or key should surface as an application error, not become a five-minute retry storm.

Here is a small Python client for the presign part of the flow. It deliberately does not send the Infrai authorization header to the returned signed URL: that URL is the customer-facing download credential. The application should store the returned payload in its own cache according to the expiry value supplied by the response.

import os
import random
import time
from typing import Any

import requests


BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def request_presigned_url(bucket: str, key: str, job_id: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.post(
            f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}",
            headers={
                "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
                "Idempotency-Key": f"export-presign:{job_id}",
                "Accept": "application/json",
            },
            timeout=10,
        )

        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            try:
                delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 0.0
            except ValueError:
                delay = 0.0
            delay = max(delay, min(30.0, 0.5 * (2**attempt)))
            time.sleep(delay + random.uniform(0, 0.25))
            continue

        if not response.ok:
            detail = response.text[:500]
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"presign request failed with HTTP {response.status_code}: {detail}"
            )

        payload = response.json()
        if not isinstance(payload, dict):
            raise RuntimeError("presign response was not a JSON object")
        return payload

    raise TimeoutError("presign rate limit did not clear after five attempts")

        bucket=os.environ["EXPORT_BUCKET"],

title: Going Cloud-Only With Laravel: What 7 Weeks on a €5 Dev Box Taught Me
summary:
Originally published at hafiz.dev

On October 12, Taylor Otwell posted that if he bought a new laptop today, he didn't think he'd install any local dev tools or languages at all. "I think I could do everything I currently do with nothing but Laravel Cloud and @AmpCode Orbs," he wrote, and said he was going to try it. The post pulled 71 replies, and three questions kept coming up. What does it cost? How do you debug when nothing runs on your machine? And can you trust what the agent ships?

I started a version of this experiment seven weeks before he posted. Not with cloud agents, though. With one €5 VPS that holds my projects, a tmux session per project, and Claude Code running inside them. I wrote up the setup and the first round of failures at the end of August.

One correction first. I'm not cloud-only, and that turned out to be the most useful finding.

Two ways to put development in the cloud

From a phone, Taylor's setup and mine look the same. A terminal, an agent, a staging URL. Underneath they're opposite shapes.

Amp's Orbs are ephemeral remote machines. Every new thread gets its own one, with the repository cloned and whatever the agent needs installed. An orb pauses when the agent goes idle, and a paused orb costs nothing. Amp's own description is that "only the diff leaves the orb." Deploys then go through Laravel Cloud, which builds from the repository.

My box keeps everything. One persistent machine, each project checked out once, a tmux session per project that survives any disconnect. The Mac and the iPhone are windows onto it. Staging runs on the box behind a Cloudflare Tunnel with an Access login in front, and production deploys go out through each project's deploy.sh.

View the interactive component on hafiz.dev

The real difference is state. An orb starts from the repository and keeps only the diff. My box holds SQLite copies of production data, queue workers that never stop, a Telegram bot that's always polling, and whatever work is in progress. That persistence is the reason the box is useful, and the cause of most of what broke.

I'm not cloud-only, and the Mac proves it

The Mac still has PHP, Composer and Node. I ran php artisan on it today. A few kinds of work never moved. NativePHP sessions run on the Mac, where the phone and the dev server share a Wi-Fi network. The repo I use for client demos stays local on purpose. So two machines still hold checkouts.

And two checkouts drift, which is why I built the box in the first place. A sync script that reports what's out of step helps. The real fix was a rule instead. A project lives in exactly one place. For anything that has moved to the box, the Mac doesn't keep a copy at all. It attaches to the box's tmux session with one alias, and the laptop becomes the same kind of window the phone is.

Push still matters, for a different reason now. The box is one machine that can die, so every project's CLAUDE.md tells the agent to pull at session start and push after every commit. Each deploy.sh also refuses to run with unpushed commits, because it ships files rather than pulling from git. Without that gate, production can end up running code that exists on no remote. That happened once.

Orbs make this whole section disappear. Nothing lives outside the repository, so there's nothing to drift. That's the first point in Taylor's favour.

What it costs after 52 days

These are the box's numbers on October 16, read straight from it:

Measure Value
Price €5 a month, VAT included
Uptime 52 days, no reboot
RAM in use 1.3 GB of 3.9 GB, with two Claude Code instances open
One Claude Code instance 330 to 355 MB resident
Swap in use 178 MB of 2 GB
Disk 15 GB of 78 GB
Load average 0.05

In August I estimated roughly 450 MB per Claude Code instance and called 4 GB the binding constraint. The real figure is lower, and the box spends most of its time waiting on the model, which is why the load average sits near zero.

Taylor's side, from the public price lists. I haven't used Orbs, so read this as a reading of pricing pages, not a review.

  • Amp's pricing page lists an Individual tier at $20 a month that includes 45,000 minutes of orb time, and tokens can come from your own Claude or ChatGPT subscription. Those minutes are counted at a1.small, the size closest to my box. That's 750 hours, which Amp says covers three at once for eight hours a day.
  • Pay-as-you-go orb rates run from $0.08 an hour (1 CPU, 2 GB) to $2.13 an hour for the largest size. The closest match to my box, a1.small with 2 CPUs and 4 GB, is $0.17 an hour.
  • Laravel Cloud's Starter plan is $5 a month plus usage, with $5 of usage credit included and compute that scales to zero.

Careful with the comparison, though. My €5 covers development only. Production runs on servers I was already paying for, which is its own trade-off and the subject of my Cloud vs Forge vs VPS breakdown. So the fair line is Amp's $20 against my €5. The gap is real and small. The other difference is the shape of the bill. Mine is flat whether I work two hours or twelve. Amp's is flat too until the included minutes run out, and orb minutes grow with hours and with parallel threads. And parallel threads are the point of orbs. They run several agents at once, each in its own machine. My box runs them side by side in one.

What broke after the first post

The August post had a table of everything that broke during setup. These came later, from daily use. Several are Laravel-specific, and a few would hit anyone working on a remote machine.

Symptom Cause Fix
Livewire buttons did nothing on a tunnelled app. No error, state never saved Laravel generated http:// URLs behind the tunnel, and Livewire's update request never landed Force the scheme and root URL in AppServiceProvider
A queued job died on a config key that was right there in the file The worker booted before the edit and still held the old config Restart the queue unit after any change, or run queue:listen
Telegram couldn't deliver webhooks to the bot Cloudflare Access guards every path, so Telegram got the login page Long polling with getUpdates from a systemd unit, no inbound route
Search Console data on one site froze for a week, silently A deploy's rsync --delete removed a production-only credential under storage/app/private Exclude storage/app/private/ wholesale in the rsync exclude file
deploy.sh said "Cannot connect to server" while the site stayed up The production box's Tailscale key had expired six days earlier, and deploy.sh connected over Tailscale Disable key expiry on servers
deploy.sh hung, then timed out on port 22 I closed public SSH on a production box, but the dev box's SSH alias still pointed at the public IP Update every client alias the day a box is hardened
cloudflared put a second domain's DNS record inside the wrong zone The cert.pem from cloudflared tunnel login is scoped to the zone picked at login Add the CNAME by hand in the other zone
Every request to Reddit returned 403 "Blocked" Reddit blocks requests from the hosting provider's IP range No direct fix. A Reddit front-end mirror loaded in headless Chromium works from the box
Playwright couldn't find its browser inside Claude Code's shell The agent's shells don't source /etc/environment, so PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH is unset Set the variable on the command itself

The Livewire one is a trusted-proxy trap

TLS ends at Cloudflare, and the tunnel hands Caddy plain HTTP. Caddy's reverse proxy, which php_fastcgi builds on, sets X-Forwarded-Proto to the scheme it saw and ignores incoming values unless the sender is a trusted proxy. So PHP receives X-Forwarded-Proto: http.

My vhosts also pass HTTPS=on to PHP-FPM, and that fixed mixed-content errors everywhere else. But this app had trustProxies(at: '*') in bootstrap/app.php, so Laravel believed the forwarded header over the server variable and generated http:// URLs. Livewire's update endpoint was one of them, so from an HTTPS page its update requests went to an http:// URL and never landed. Nothing logged an error.

The fix that's running now, on Laravel 13.30 with Livewire 4:

// app/Providers/AppServiceProvider.php
public function boot(): void
{
    // TLS ends at Cloudflare and the tunnel hands Caddy plain http. Every
    // generated URL (Livewire update endpoint included) must still be https,
    // or Always-Use-HTTPS turns Livewire's POST into a dead GET.
    if (str_starts_with((string) config('app.url'), 'https://')) {
        \Illuminate\Support\Facades\URL::forceScheme('https');
        \Illuminate\Support\Facades\URL::forceRootUrl(config('app.url'));
    }
}

The guard on app.url keeps a plain http://localhost setup working.

The queue worker one gets worse on a dev box

In production, the deploy restarts the workers. On a dev box nothing deploys. You edit config/services.php, the worker running under systemd keeps the config it booted with, and the next job reads the new key as null. Mine died like this:

array_map(): Argument #2 ($array) must be of type array, null given

The queue docs explain why. Workers "store the booted application state in memory" and "will not notice changes in your code base after they have been started." There are two ways out. Restart the unit after every code or config change, which is what I do now. Or run queue:listen on the dev box, which reloads your code for each job and is, in the docs' words, "significantly less efficient."

The trust question, seven weeks in

The August FAQ covered production deploy keys on a box with an agent on it. What's new is isolation between projects.

When the Telegram bot needed its own agent login and its own credentials, sharing root's was wrong and sharing www-data's wasn't much better. It got a dedicated system user, its own PHP-FPM pool on its own socket, its own queue unit and its own cron line. And it's deliberately kept out of the www-data group, because the other projects' .env files are group-readable.

That's isolation an orb gives you for free. Each thread is its own machine, and only the diff comes out. On a shared box, you build isolation per project, by hand, after you notice you need it.

The maintenance nobody demos

While I was collecting the numbers above, the box reported a pending reboot. It's running kernel 6.12.101. Three kernel updates have landed since it booted, and the newest, 6.12.111, is installed and waiting. I found the same trap on a production server in September, where unattended upgrades had installed five kernels that never ran. Uptime looks great on a status page. It also means the running kernel is whatever booted last.

Then there's the Tailscale key row in the table. The default node key expiry is 180 days, and when it passes, "connections to/from the given endpoint will stop working." On a server with SSH locked to the tailnet, that's admin access gone while the site keeps serving. The production boxes I hardened in September have expiry disabled now, and so does the dev box.

None of this is hard. But it's mine to remember. With orbs and Laravel Cloud, patching and access are the provider's job.

Where each setup wins

Taylor's setup wins on these:

  • Isolation per task, and several agents running in parallel
  • No drift, because nothing exists outside the repository
  • No box to patch, reboot or keep reachable
  • Git-based deploys, which remove the whole rsync --delete class of failure

The box wins on these:

  • A flat €5 whatever the hours
  • State that outlives a thread, like production data copies, a bot that polls all day and workers that are always up
  • Root, any language, any tool, at no extra cost
  • Staging on real data behind a login, without a per-environment price

If your work is one or two apps already on Laravel Cloud, Taylor's setup removes failure classes I spent seven weeks fixing by hand. If you run several small apps on your own VPSes, with SQLite and long-running processes, one persistent box is cheaper and fits that shape better. I'm keeping the box.

FAQ

Can you run Laravel queue workers on a remote dev box?

Yes, with one habit. Workers keep the application state they booted with, so restart the worker's unit after any code or config change. If you'd rather not think about it, run php artisan queue:listen on the dev box instead. It reloads code for every job at a performance cost that rarely matters in development.

How much RAM does a dev box running Claude Code need?

On mine, two Claude Code instances use 330 to 355 MB each, and the whole box uses 1.3 GB of 4 GB with a tmux session per project. A 2 GB swap file covers spikes from composer install and npm run build. 4 GB is comfortable for a few agents at once.

Why do Livewire actions fail silently behind Cloudflare Tunnel?

Usually because Laravel generates http:// URLs. With trustProxies(at: '*'), Laravel trusts X-Forwarded-Proto, and a local proxy behind the tunnel may report http. Livewire then sends its updates from an https:// page to an http:// URL, and they never reach the component. Forcing the scheme and root URL in AppServiceProvider::boot() fixes it.

Are Amp Orbs cheaper than a VPS for Laravel development?

Not on the price list. Amp's Individual tier is $20 a month with 45,000 orb minutes (750 hours at the 4 GB size), against €5 for a 4 GB VPS. Orbs buy isolation, parallel agents and zero maintenance. A VPS buys persistent state and a flat bill. I haven't used Orbs, so this comes from Amp's published pricing.

The real bill

Money was never the expensive part. Attention was. Orbs take most of that off your plate for $20 a month instead of €5, and Laravel Cloud takes the rest on its own bill. Whether that's worth it depends on one question. Do your projects need state that outlives a thread? Mine do.
